problems.title: Entropy change of heated water
problems.scenario:
**10 kg** of liquid water is heated from **20 °C** to **80 °C**. Take $c = 4.18\ \text{kJ/(kg·K)}$.

Find the **entropy change** of the water, in kJ/K.
hints: For an incompressible substance, $\Delta S = m\,c\,\ln(T_2/T_1)$.
problems.solution:
Water is incompressible, so its entropy change depends only on the temperature ratio:

$$\Delta S = m\,c\,\ln\frac{T_2}{T_1} = 10 \times 4.18 \times \ln\frac{353}{293}$$

$$\Delta S = 41.8 \times \ln(1.2048) = 41.8 \times 0.1864 = 7.79\ \text{kJ/K}$$

The logarithm needs **absolute** temperatures — a ratio of °C values would be wrong.

problems.title: Isentropic temperature rise
problems.scenario:
Air at **300 K** and **100 kPa** is compressed **isentropically** to **600 kPa**. Take $k = 1.4$.

Find the **exit temperature**, in K.
hints: Use the isentropic $T$–$P$ relation for an ideal gas.
problems.solution:
For an isentropic process with constant specific heats:

$$T_2 = T_1\left(\frac{P_2}{P_1}\right)^{(k-1)/k} = 300\left(\frac{600}{100}\right)^{0.4/1.4}$$

$$T_2 = 300 \times 6^{0.2857} = 300 \times 1.6685 = 500.6\ \text{K}$$

Compressing a gas isentropically always raises its temperature.

problems.title: Entropy change of air (T, P known)
problems.scenario:
Air changes from **300 K, 100 kPa** to **500 K, 500 kPa**. Take $c_p = 1.005$ and $R = 0.287\ \text{kJ/(kg·K)}$.

Find the **specific entropy change** $\Delta s$, in kJ/(kg·K).
hints: With temperature and pressure given, use the $(T,P)$ form.
The pressure term is *subtracted* — rising pressure lowers entropy.
problems.solution:
Choose the entropy form that matches the given data ($T$ and $P$):

$$\Delta s = c_p\ln\frac{T_2}{T_1} - R\ln\frac{P_2}{P_1}$$

Evaluate each term:

$$c_p\ln\frac{T_2}{T_1} = 1.005\ln\frac{500}{300} = 1.005 \times 0.5108 = 0.5134$$

$$R\ln\frac{P_2}{P_1} = 0.287\ln 5 = 0.287 \times 1.6094 = 0.4619$$

$$\Delta s = 0.5134 - 0.4619 = 0.0515\ \text{kJ/(kg·K)}$$

The heating raises entropy while the compression lowers it; here the net is slightly positive.

problems.title: Isentropic expansion (volume ratio)
problems.scenario:
Air at **800 K** expands isentropically until its volume is **8 times** larger ($v_2/v_1 = 8$). Take $k = 1.4$.

Find the **final temperature**, in K.
hints: Note the volume ratio is inverted ($v_1/v_2 = 1/8$).
problems.solution:
For an isentropic process the temperature–volume relation is:

$$T_2 = T_1\left(\frac{v_1}{v_2}\right)^{k-1} = 800\left(\frac{1}{8}\right)^{0.4}$$

$$T_2 = 800 \times (0.125)^{0.4} = 800 \times 0.4353 = 348.2\ \text{K}$$

Expanding a gas isentropically cools it — the basis of how a turbine drops temperature.

problems.title: Entropy generation in heat transfer
problems.scenario:
**500 kJ** of heat is transferred directly from a source at **800 K** to a sink at **300 K**.

Find the total **entropy generated**, in kJ/K.
hints: Each reservoir changes entropy by $Q/T$: the sink gains $+Q/T_L$, the source loses $-Q/T_H$.
problems.solution:
Heat leaves the source (entropy $-Q/T_H$) and enters the sink (entropy $+Q/T_L$). The total entropy change of everything is the generation:

$$S_{gen} = \frac{Q}{T_L} - \frac{Q}{T_H} = \frac{500}{300} - \frac{500}{800}$$

$$S_{gen} = 1.6667 - 0.625 = 1.042\ \text{kJ/K}$$

It's positive, as the second law demands — heat flowing across a finite temperature difference is irreversible and *generates* entropy.

problems.title: Turbine isentropic efficiency
problems.scenario:
Steam enters a turbine at $h_1 = 3231\ \text{kJ/kg}$. For an isentropic expansion to the exit pressure, the exit enthalpy would be $h_{2s} = 2200\ \text{kJ/kg}$. The turbine's isentropic efficiency is **0.85**.

Find the **actual work output** per kg, in kJ/kg.
hints: Isentropic (ideal) work is the enthalpy drop to $h_{2s}$: $w_s = h_1 - h_{2s}$.
Turbine efficiency = actual work ÷ ideal work, so $w_{act} = \eta_T (h_1 - h_{2s})$.
problems.solution:
The ideal (isentropic) work is the full enthalpy drop to $h_{2s}$:

$$w_s = h_1 - h_{2s} = 3231 - 2200 = 1031\ \text{kJ/kg}$$

The real turbine delivers a fraction $\eta_T$ of that:

$$w_{act} = \eta_T\,(h_1 - h_{2s}) = 0.85 \times 1031 = 876.4\ \text{kJ/kg}$$

Irreversibilities mean the actual exit enthalpy is higher (less work extracted) than the ideal case.

problems.title: Compressor isentropic efficiency
problems.scenario:
Air enters a compressor at $h_1 = 300.19\ \text{kJ/kg}$. The isentropic (ideal) exit enthalpy is $h_{2s} = 430.0\ \text{kJ/kg}$. The compressor's isentropic efficiency is **0.80**.

Find the **actual work input** per kg, in kJ/kg.
hints: For a compressor the efficiency ratio is *inverted* vs a turbine: $\eta_C = w_s/w_{act}$.
problems.solution:
For a compressor, the *ideal* (isentropic) work is the smaller one, so efficiency is ideal ÷ actual:

$$\eta_C = \frac{h_{2s} - h_1}{h_2 - h_1} = \frac{w_s}{w_{act}} \quad\Rightarrow\quad w_{act} = \frac{h_{2s} - h_1}{\eta_C}$$

The ideal work:

$$w_s = h_{2s} - h_1 = 430.0 - 300.19 = 129.81\ \text{kJ/kg}$$

So the actual input is larger:

$$w_{act} = \frac{129.81}{0.80} = 162.3\ \text{kJ/kg}$$

Note the efficiency ratio flips between turbines (actual/ideal) and compressors (ideal/actual) — getting this backwards is a classic mistake.

problems.title: Entropy generated by mixing water
problems.scenario:
**2 kg** of water at **80 °C** is mixed with **2 kg** of water at **20 °C** in an insulated container. Take $c = 4.18\ \text{kJ/(kg·K)}$.

Find the **entropy generated** by the mixing, in kJ/K.
hints: Equal masses, same fluid → equilibrium temperature is the average: $T_{eq} = (353 + 293)/2 = 323\ \text{K}$.
Each stream's entropy change is $m c \ln(T_{eq}/T_i)$; sum them.
problems.solution:
**Step 1 — equilibrium temperature.** Equal masses of the same fluid average out:

$$T_{eq} = \frac{T_1 + T_2}{2} = \frac{353 + 293}{2} = 323\ \text{K}$$

**Step 2 — entropy change of each stream**, summed (insulated → no entropy transfer, so the total *is* the generation):

$$S_{gen} = m c\ln\frac{T_{eq}}{T_1} + m c\ln\frac{T_{eq}}{T_2}$$

$$S_{gen} = 2(4.18)\left[\ln\frac{323}{353} + \ln\frac{323}{293}\right] = 8.36\,[-0.0888 + 0.0975]$$

$$S_{gen} = 8.36 \times 0.00869 = 0.073\ \text{kJ/K}$$

The hot stream *loses* entropy and the cold one *gains* more, so the total is positive — mixing is irreversible.

problems.title: Real turbine work via isentropic efficiency
problems.scenario:
Air expands through an **adiabatic turbine** from **700 kPa, 750 K** to **100 kPa**, with an isentropic efficiency of **0.88**. Take $c_p = 1.005$, $R = 0.287\ \text{kJ/(kg·K)}$, $k = 1.4$.

Find the **actual specific work output**, in kJ/kg.
problems.solution:
**Step 1 — isentropic exit temperature** $((k-1)/k = 0.2857)$:

$$T_{2s} = 750\left(\frac{100}{700}\right)^{0.2857} = 750 \times 0.5735 = 430.1\ \text{K}$$

**Step 2 — ideal (isentropic) work:**

$$w_s = c_p(T_1 - T_{2s}) = 1.005(750 - 430.1) = 321.5\ \text{kJ/kg}$$

**Step 3 — actual work** via the isentropic efficiency:

$$w = \eta_T\, w_s = 0.88 \times 321.5 = 283\ \text{kJ/kg}$$

problems.title: A reversible air conditioner: zero net entropy
problems.scenario:
A **completely reversible** air conditioner provides **36,000 Btu/h** of cooling to a space kept at **70°F**, rejecting heat to outdoor air at **110°F**.

Find the **rate of entropy increase of the outdoor air** (the hot reservoir), in Btu/(h·R).
hints: Convert both temperatures to Rankine: add 459.67.
For a *reversible* device, $\dot Q_H/T_H = \dot Q_L/T_L$ — use this to find $\dot Q_H$ first.
Then the hot reservoir's entropy gain is simply $\dot S_H = \dot Q_H/T_H$.
problems.solution:
**Convert to Rankine:** $T_L = 70+459.67 = 529.67\ \text{R}$, $T_H = 110+459.67 = 569.67\ \text{R}$.

**Find the heat rejected**, using the reversible-cycle relation $\dot Q_H/T_H = \dot Q_L/T_L$:

$$\dot Q_H = \dot Q_L\,\frac{T_H}{T_L} = 36{,}000\times\frac{569.67}{529.67} = 38{,}719\ \text{Btu/h}$$

**Entropy rate of the hot reservoir** (it only *receives* heat, so this is simple):

$$\dot S_H = \frac{\dot Q_H}{T_H} = \frac{38{,}719}{569.67} = 67.97\ \text{Btu/(h·R)}$$

The cold space loses entropy at exactly $\dot S_L = -\dot Q_L/T_L = -67.97\ \text{Btu/(h·R)}$ — for this **reversible** device the two exactly cancel, giving **zero** net entropy generation, right at the second-law limit. Any real (irreversible) air conditioner would generate a small positive total.

problems.title: Entropy rate during isothermal compression
problems.scenario:
A compressor draws **40 kW** of power to compress air from $P_1$ to $P_2$. The air temperature is held **constant at 25°C** throughout, because heat is continuously rejected to the surroundings during the compression.

Find the **rate of entropy change of the air**, in kW/K.
hints: The air's temperature doesn't change, so for an ideal gas $\Delta u = 0$ — use the energy balance to find the heat transfer rate first.
$\dot Q - \dot W = \Delta \dot U = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \dot Q = \dot W$. With 40 kW of work going *into* the air, heat must leave the air at the same rate.
For an internally reversible process at *constant* temperature, entropy change is simply $\dot S = \dot Q/T$ — no need for the pressure ratio at all.
problems.solution:
**Find the heat transfer rate.** Since the temperature doesn't change and air is an ideal gas, its internal energy doesn't change either: $\Delta \dot U = 0$. The energy balance then gives:

$$\dot Q - \dot W = \Delta \dot U = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \dot Q = \dot W$$

Work is done *on* the air (compression), so from the air's perspective $\dot W = -40\ \text{kW}$, and therefore $\dot Q = -40\ \text{kW}$ — heat leaves the air at 40 kW, exactly balancing the work put in.

**Entropy rate.** For a process at constant temperature, the entropy change is $\dot S = \dot Q/T$ directly — you don't need to know the pressure ratio at all:

$$\dot S_{air} = \frac{\dot Q}{T} = \frac{-40}{298.15} = -0.134\ \text{kW/K}$$

The air's entropy *falls* as it's compressed — consistent with $\Delta s = -R\ln(P_2/P_1)$, which would give the identical answer if you worked it out from the pressure ratio instead.

problems.title: Entropy change with variable specific heats (s° table)
problems.scenario:
Air is compressed from **100 kPa, 17°C** (290 K) to **600 kPa, 57°C** (330 K). Rather than assume constant specific heats, use the **exact** air-table method.

From Table A-17: $s^\circ(290\ \text{K}) = 1.66802$ and $s^\circ(330\ \text{K}) = 1.79783\ \text{kJ/(kg·K)}$. Take $R = 0.287\ \text{kJ/(kg·K)}$.

Find the specific entropy change $\Delta s$, in kJ/(kg·K).
hints: Use the exact (variable-specific-heat) form: $\Delta s = s_2^\circ - s_1^\circ - R\ln(P_2/P_1)$.
$s^\circ$ already accounts for the temperature change; the log term adds the pressure effect.
problems.solution:
The exact method reads the temperature part of entropy from the table ($s^\circ$) and adds the pressure term:

$$\Delta s = s_2^\circ - s_1^\circ - R\ln\frac{P_2}{P_1}$$

$$= (1.79783 - 1.66802) - 0.287\ln\frac{600}{100} = 0.12981 - 0.287(1.7918)$$

$$= 0.12981 - 0.51424 = -0.384\ \text{kJ/(kg·K)}$$

The entropy *decreases* because the pressure rise (which lowers entropy) outweighs the small temperature rise. Here $\Delta T$ is small so constant-$c_p$ would give nearly the same answer — but for large $\Delta T$ this $s^\circ$ method is the accurate one to use.

problems.title: Isentropic compression via relative specific volume
problems.scenario:
Air is compressed **isentropically** in a car engine from **22°C** (295 K), with a compression ratio $V_1/V_2 = 8$. Because the temperature change is large, use the **relative specific volume** method (variable specific heats).

From Table A-17, at 295 K the relative specific volume is $v_{r1} = 647.9$.

Find $v_{r2}$ at the final state. *(You would then read $T_2$ off the table at this $v_r$ — the book gives $T_2 = 662.7$ K.)*
problems.solution:
The relative specific volume tracks the isentropic volume ratio directly:

$$\frac{v_2}{v_1} = \frac{v_{r2}}{v_{r1}} \quad\Rightarrow\quad v_{r2} = v_{r1}\,\frac{v_2}{v_1} = 647.9\times\frac{1}{8} = 80.99$$

Reading the air table at $v_r = 80.99$ gives $T_2 = 662.7$ K — so the air heats up by about 368°C during compression. Using the constant-$k$ relation $T_2 = T_1(V_1/V_2)^{k-1} = 295(8)^{0.4} = 677$ K would be a few percent off, because $k$ isn't really constant over such a large temperature rise. The $v_r$ method avoids that error.

problems.title: Compressor work: isentropic vs isothermal
problems.scenario:
Air is compressed steadily and reversibly from **100 kPa, 300 K** to **900 kPa** in a piston-free steady-flow compressor. Take $R = 0.287\ \text{kJ/(kg·K)}$, $k = 1.4$.

Find the work input, in kJ/kg, for **isentropic** compression. *(Compare it in your solution to the isothermal case.)*
problems.solution:
Apply the reversible isentropic compressor-work relation:

$$w = \frac{kRT_1}{k-1}\left[\left(\frac{P_2}{P_1}\right)^{(k-1)/k} - 1\right] = \frac{1.4\times0.287\times300}{0.4}\left[9^{0.2857} - 1\right]$$

$$= 301.35\times(1.8734 - 1) = 301.35\times0.8734 = 263\ \text{kJ/kg}$$

By comparison, **isothermal** compression over the same pressure ratio needs only $w = RT\ln(P_2/P_1) = 0.287\times300\times\ln 9 = 189\ \text{kJ/kg}$ — about 28% less. The isothermal path keeps the specific volume small (via cooling), and since $w \propto \int v\,dP$, that directly cuts the work. This is the whole motivation for intercooling.

problems.title: Two-stage compression with intercooling
problems.scenario:
Air is compressed from **100 kPa, 300 K** to **900 kPa** using **ideal two-stage compression with intercooling** back to 300 K between stages. Each stage is polytropic with $n = 1.3$. Take $R = 0.287\ \text{kJ/(kg·K)}$.

Find the **total** work input, in kJ/kg. *(First find the optimal intermediate pressure.)*
hints: Optimal intermediate pressure (equal pressure ratio per stage): $P_x = \sqrt{P_1 P_2} = \sqrt{100\times900}$.
Each stage has the same pressure ratio $P_x/P_1 = 3$, and (with intercooling to the same $T_1$) does the same work.
problems.solution:
**Step 1 — optimal intermediate pressure** (the geometric mean minimizes total work):

$$P_x = \sqrt{P_1 P_2} = \sqrt{100\times900} = 300\ \text{kPa}$$

Each stage then has pressure ratio $P_x/P_1 = P_2/P_x = 3$.

**Step 2 — total work.** With intercooling back to $T_1 = 300$ K, both stages start at the same temperature and do identical work:

$$w = 2\times\frac{nRT_1}{n-1}\left[\left(\frac{P_x}{P_1}\right)^{(n-1)/n} - 1\right] = 2\times\frac{1.3\times0.287\times300}{0.3}\left[3^{0.2308} - 1\right]$$

$$= 2\times373.1\times(1.2887 - 1) = 2\times373.1\times0.2887 = 215\ \text{kJ/kg}$$

Single-stage polytropic compression to 900 kPa would need about 246 kJ/kg, so intercooling saves ~31 kJ/kg — it pulls the work down toward the isothermal limit.

problems.title: Nozzle isentropic efficiency → exit velocity
problems.scenario:
Air at **200 kPa, 950 K** enters an adiabatic nozzle at low velocity and discharges at **110 kPa**. The nozzle's isentropic efficiency is **0.92**. Use high-temperature averages $k = 1.349$ and $c_p = 1.11\ \text{kJ/(kg·K)}$.

Find the **actual exit velocity**, in m/s.
hints: Step 1: isentropic exit temperature $T_{2s} = T_1(P_2/P_1)^{(k-1)/k}$, with $(k-1)/k = 0.349/1.349$.
Step 2: ideal exit velocity from energy balance $V_{2s} = \sqrt{2c_p(T_1 - T_{2s})}$ (mind the ×1000 for kJ→J).
problems.solution:
**Step 1 — isentropic exit temperature:**

$$T_{2s} = T_1\left(\frac{P_2}{P_1}\right)^{(k-1)/k} = 950\left(\frac{110}{200}\right)^{0.349/1.349} = 950\times0.857 = 814\ \text{K}$$

**Step 2 — ideal (isentropic) exit velocity** from the adiabatic energy balance $h_1 = h_2 + V_2^2/2$ with negligible inlet velocity:

$$V_{2s} = \sqrt{2c_p(T_1 - T_{2s})} = \sqrt{2\times1.11\times(950-814)\times1000} = \sqrt{301{,}920} = 549\ \text{m/s}$$

(the ×1000 converts kJ/kg to m²/s²).

**Step 3 — actual exit velocity** from the nozzle efficiency ($\eta_N = V_{2a}^2/V_{2s}^2$):

$$V_{2a} = \sqrt{\eta_N}\,V_{2s} = \sqrt{0.92}\times549 = 527\ \text{m/s}$$

Friction makes the real jet slower (and the exit gas ~11 K hotter) than the isentropic ideal — kinetic energy that was lost to irreversibility.
